claims.text: The starting material is equimolar or near-equimolar CoCrFeNiTi.
The starting CoCrFeNiTi is a coarse-grained, single-phase solid solution at room temperature.
Coarse grain size and the single-phase solid-solution state govern the relatively low hardness and strength of CoCrFeNiTi.
The coarse-grained single-phase structure permits relatively unhindered dislocation glide.
The lattice-distortion effect in equimolar or near-equimolar CoCrFeNiTi is moderate.
Nanocrystalline grain-boundary strengthening and strengthening by secondary precipitates are absent from the starting CoCrFeNiTi.
High hardness and compressive strength in other high-entropy alloys can arise from nanocrystalline grain sizes or hard secondary phases.
Cr addition to HfMoTaTiZr produced a Laves phase together with increased hardness and yield strength.
The cited CuMoTaWV film had a nanocrystalline BCC solid solution with an average grain size of 18 nm.
Grain size and nanoscale precipitates mediate a transition from dislocation-dominated deformation to grain-boundary or precipitate-hardening mechanisms.
Increasing grain-boundary density by refining grains impedes dislocation glide.
Introducing dispersed precipitates increases barrier density and impedes dislocation glide.
Grain-refined CoCrFeNiTi will have greater hardness and compressive strength than the coarse-grained starting state.
Precipitate-enhanced CoCrFeNiTi will have greater hardness and compressive strength than the single-phase starting state.
The strengthening caused by grain refinement or precipitates will likely reduce ductility.
Hardness and compressive strength should correlate inversely with grain size.
Hardness and compressive strength should correlate directly with precipitate volume fraction.
The hypothesis is limited to quasi-static hardness or compression loading from room temperature through 600 °C.
The hypothesis may not apply to initially multiphase alloys or very dynamic loading.

contradictions.description: Reduced ductility is described only as likely or potential, but the falsification rule treats failure to observe a ductility decrease as sufficient to falsify the core strength mechanism.
